summary: Discusses point-to-point and multi-endpoint topologies in RTP environments, and maps the central topologies common in video conferencing to RTP terminology.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP conferences can connect participants directly, through multicast, or through middleboxes that relay, translate, mix, or select media. Each arrangement changes what participants can see and how control messages travel. This RFC gives those arrangements names and compares their properties.

subtitle: How RTP media and control traffic behave across conferencing topologies.

tldr.problem: Industry terms such as Multipoint Control Unit (MCU) do not say exactly how a conferencing device handles RTP media and RTCP control messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes point-to-point, multicast, mesh, translator, mixer, selective-forwarding, and MCU topologies, comparing how they handle streams, source identifiers, and control traffic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7667 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 5117. It explains topologies but does not change the requirements in RFC 3550.

today: RFC 7667 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 5117. The unit metadata lists no RFC that later obsoletes or updates it; the document says it does not change RFC 3550.

sections.title: Why RTP Topologies Need Names
sections.content:
RTP topologies describe how endpoints connect and how RTP and its control protocol, RTCP, are handled. RFC 7667 clarifies industry terms such as Multipoint Control Unit (MCU), whose media behavior may correspond to different RTP roles.

The document adds topologies, including selective forwarding, and replaces RFC 5117. It is an informal explanation and does not change what RFC 3550 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: Conference systems use many kinds of middleboxes, but the same name can describe different behavior. This RFC labels the topologies by how they handle media and control traffic.

sections.title: Translators and Mixers
sections.content:
A translator creates a separate output stream for each input stream and keeps the stream's SSRC. A transport translator changes transport details; a media translator changes the media, for example by converting it to another codec.

A mixer may select or combine incoming media, but it sends the output under its own SSRC and may list contributing sources in the CSRC field. A media translator that changes encoded output must also adjust RTCP reports so their sequence information reflects the translated stream.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator changes transport details or media while keeping each source stream distinct. A mixer selects or combines media and sends a new stream under its own source identifier.

sections.title: Direct, Multicast, and Mesh Connections
sections.content:
In point-to-point RTP, two endpoints send RTP and RTCP directly to each other. Any-Source Multicast lets group members send to the group, while Source-Specific Multicast has a designated distribution source; receivers send RTCP feedback by unicast to a feedback target.

In a mesh, each endpoint sends separate unicast flows to the others. A joint RTP session gives participants a common view but requires each sender to adapt to the least-capable path. Independent RTP sessions permit separate adaptation, but participants lose a shared view and RTP identifiers no longer provide loop detection across sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Direct, multicast, and mesh designs distribute the same media in different ways. A shared session gives endpoints a common view; separate sessions let each path adapt independently but hide conditions on other paths.

sections.title: Mixers, Selective Forwarding, and MCUs
sections.content:
A media-mixing mixer decodes streams, combines or tiles them, and encodes a new stream. This uses processing resources and can add delay or reduce quality. A media-switching mixer forwards a selected encoded stream under its own SSRC, rewriting RTP header fields to keep the outgoing stream coherent.

A Selective Forwarding Middlebox makes possible sources available to each endpoint and chooses which sources send. It can have low delay, but endpoints need to handle multiple sources or switch decoder state efficiently. The RFC also explains that common RTCP-terminating MCU behavior breaks RTP-level participant identification when it omits contributing-source information.
sections.plainLanguage: A mixing device rebuilds a combined stream, while a switching device forwards a selected encoded stream. A selective-forwarding device chooses which source streams reach each endpoint.

sections.title: Security Effects of Middleboxes
sections.content:
Mixers, selective-forwarding middleboxes, and media translators modify packets. To do so in a protected session, they generally need to be trusted participants in the security context and have the required keys.

A compromised middlebox inside that context can attack a session while participants believe it is protected. A transport translator that leaves protected RTP content unchanged may work without access to payload keys, but other middleboxes need cryptographic processing to change protected media.
sections.plainLanguage: A middlebox that changes protected media needs access to the security context. If that device is compromised, it can misuse the access while the endpoints believe the session is protected.
